title: ​Ectovox on the changing role of storytelling in water parks
summary:
Water parks are becoming more than collections of slides and pools. As guest expectations evolve, operators are creating destinations that combine aquatic attractions with storytelling, theming and immersive experiences.

That shift is changing design's role in water park development. For Ectovox, the answer is to bring creative development and engineering together from the outset, combining narrative, visual design and planning with the technical expertise needed to deliver complex aquatic environments.

Based in Orlando, Ectovox grew out of Martin Aquatic’s concept studio and became its own experiential design division. It works across water parks, resort amenities, cruise and other location-based entertainment projects.


Ectovox’s multidisciplinary team includes storytellers, graphic artists, 3D modellers and interior designers alongside aquatic engineers and master planners.

Its projects range from cruise destinations and expansions to indoor water parks built around established brands, including Mattel and Hasbro. The goal is to develop aquatic destinations as complete experiences, considering the creative concept and physical environment together.

​From Martin Aquatic to Ectovox


In 2019, Martin Aquatic’s in-house creative team led a corporate rebrand and created the Martin Aquatic identity. The work attracted attention from developers and others in the industry, who began asking who was behind it.

The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 disrupted development schedules across the industry, but it also let the company explore how its creative team could support clients beyond traditional aquatic design and engineering.


As demand grew for branding, digital artwork, and marketing, the creative team became a more formal offering and eventually became Ectovox, a division focused on experiential design, storytelling, and master planning.

An early collaboration with themed entertainment specialist Chris Grap, now VP of Ectovox at Martin Aquatic, helped shape the direction. At the time, Grap was vice president of experiential development at Mall of America and was working with the team on Mystery Cove.

“Chris was both a client and a friend working with Mall of America at the time on Mystery Cove, and we got a really good flavour of our ability to work together,” says Josh Martin, president and creative director at Martin Aquatic.


“That led us to go, 'Hey, we'd like to do more of this work.' Now our focus has largely been on taking these destinations and creating the full experiential design. It really goes back to storytelling.”

Grap says the new division gave the work a clearer identity and allowed the team to pursue a wider range of projects.

"When you hear Martin Aquatic, that is broad, but it's limiting in the sense of when you start to think about experiential design and guest experience. The team had been doing this work but really wasn't getting credit or recognition for it.

“What I think Ectovox does is allow for a wider scope that branches a bit more outside what you would have expected from Martin Aquatic, and it's been interesting to see the opportunities that have come our way from it.”

​Bringing creative design and engineering together


Ectovox brings market research, master planning and creative development together from the beginning of a project.

An in-house team of market researchers conducts competitor and feasibility benchmarking; Martin leads designers focused on master planning, spatial layout, and operational flow, while Grap focuses on thematic narrative and character development.

The team includes mechanical engineers, interior designers, former show-set construction specialists, graphic artists, 3D animators and computational fluid dynamics experts. This allows the team to consider creative ideas alongside commercial, operational, and technical requirements.


Martin says: “We like to say internally we do constructable concepts. A client may have a really creative vision, and we want to help execute that. But we're also going, 'It doesn't fit your budget,' or 'It doesn't fit the ability to build this'.

“We spend that time telling that story, and we love doing it from a research lens with benchmarking, because a lot of clients will say, 'Oh, I want what this guy has.' Well, why do you want the same thing that he has?

"Let's come up with something more original, more creative, and now we're adding that level of story and theming and guest journey on top of it.”

Grap adds: “To me, this is one of the closest things to filmmaking, where all the disciplines come together, bringing the best in your field, and landing together on a project.”


Engineering can also inform the creative experience. Martin gives the example of an aquatic attraction designed around changes in water speed and movement.

"Our creatives have access to our smartest engineers. We have a guy on our team who does computational fluid dynamics modelling, and he’s brilliant at it. Our designers have ideas like, 'Hey, I want to do this with an action river,' and he'll work out a solution or a simulation and say, 'This is how you do it.'

“One of our team members spent months simulating a river as part of a creative story to tell the guest journey, with slow-down moments, speed-up moments, and waves being introduced.

“That is how we make engineering very much a part of the creative journey.”

This integration can also identify construction, budget and regulatory issues before a concept progresses too far.

Grap says: "That's the concept working with engineering to truly make it a reality versus putting something in front of a guest that might look pretty on a page but can't be delivered. It's that type of resource in the toolbox that elevates the entire project.”

See also: Blue Mar Wellness from Martin Aquatic

​Applying theme park thinking to water parks


Ectovox aims to bring theme park storytelling and environmental detail into water parks, creating different levels of engagement in the same space.

Grap says the approach starts with treating water park guests like theme park visitors.

"As a guest for years, I saw water parks not develop in tandem with theme parks; before working directly with Martin Aquatic, my approach was, 'I don't want to design a water park. I want to design a theme park with water-based attractions.'

“How do we make the space feel more lived in? How do we make it feel more active? Why can't we put this type of attraction in here just because it hasn't been done before? We really try to think of the environment as a whole, give it life and movement, and treat guests the same way you would a theme park guest."


“Some people just want the attractions; others want the story; and some want to know absolutely everything, and we want to satisfy all of them. We've said this for years: we're not designing for one visit; we're designing for your twentieth visit. The more we can add that enrichment and detail, the more enjoyable it's going to be across the board.

“Even if you're not paying attention to it, you're going to feel it.”

The philosophy is shaping Ectovox's work with Mattel, says Martin:

“With the work we're doing with Mattel right now, there are a lot of Easter eggs and hidden moments planned so that if you know the brands, we have something for you. When you look at it, we want to make sure we represent all those different moments, because guests notice different things.”


The team also uses visits to attractions and resorts as research, studying environmental detailing, show-set construction and guest movement. Martin calls these visits a ‘splash-about’:

"We look at some of the work we've done and orient new team members. When we say show set or dimensional flat, what do we actually mean? Looking at those items helps our team keep moving with that shared shorthand.

“What's great about our team across engineering and creative is that we have a bunch of really passionate people. We are very much bespoke creative every time.”

​Creating an African oasis at Hattiesburg Zoo


One of Ectovox’s early projects was Serengeti Springs, a water park expansion at Hattiesburg Zoo in Mississippi.

Martin Aquatic initially handled master planning and engineering, but as the project progressed, the zoo identified another need: a name, brand, and story for the new attraction.

Located alongside the zoo’s African animal habitats, the water park offered an opportunity to connect the two experiences. Ectovox helped develop it as an African oasis, giving the attraction its own identity while linking it to the surrounding zoo.


Martin says the team became involved late in the process.

"Serengeti Springs was a project where we did the master plan and design, and we were almost through full engineered documents when the client said, 'We don't have a name. What are we going to do?' I was in a meeting in Hattiesburg and said, 'Well, we have this division called Ectovox.'

“I introduced them, and two of our designers flew up to Mississippi and went through the guest journey and experience with that client to create a great logo and backstory. They had a great asset in their zoo, and the water park was adjacent to their Africa expansion, where you could literally look into their giraffe barn.

“They didn’t have the largest budget in the world, but they had so much passion and really wanted to put that extra level of detail into it.”

A post shared by Serengeti Springs at the Hattiesburg Zoo (@serengeti.springs)

Creative development extended beyond the name and logo. Ectovox worked with attraction supplier WhiteWater to adapt catalogue play structures to the theme.

Martin says: "The leadership in Hattiesburg told us, 'We want people to just forget that they're in Mississippi. How can I make Mississippi feel like an oasis where visitors can be completely transported?'

"Using that as a guide for the theme and name made it a really collaborative effort. What was great was how willing they were to take our concepts and run with them.”

Ectovox also produced a brand book and style guide, enabling the zoo to apply the identity across signage, merchandise and marketing.

​Translating Mattel's brands into aquatic experiences


Ectovox’s work with Mattel brings its approach to narrative and creative development into a branded indoor water park concept.

Mattel Wonder is planned as a series of permanent aquatic destinations built around the toy company’s brand portfolio. The first location, in Bellevue, Nebraska, is scheduled to open at the end of 2027.

The project involves more than translating familiar characters and products into a physical setting. The team must balance established brand guidelines with the technical demands of permanent aquatic environments, including chlorine, humidity, safety and maintenance.


Grap says the process involves helping established brands consider how their properties can work in a new environment.

"Working with a legacy brand that knows their brands one way, it's about helping them explore how these brands should and can exist in an entirely new environment. It's not as simple as a direct pull of just making that toy larger.

"It is about how guests want to engage with your brand versus how the brand may be perceived, and finding that middle ground.

“It's not just about scaling up; it's about the opportunity we can present. This isn't a temporary location that changes in a year; this is going to be here for decades, and we want to make sure we are delivering something that creates core memories for guests.”


Martin says the project also involves explaining the practical requirements of aquatic environments to the brand owners.

“Mattel and Hasbro are fantastic at making toys, but neither of them are water park or theme park operators at this stage in their companies. There's been an element of teaching what the guest will see, pointing out elements high up in the sky, and explaining what can actually survive in an aquatic environment.

“We have chlorine, splashes, safety regulations, and ASTM standards that you don't want to get in the way of creativity, but you have to make them aware of those elements. When you do permanent installations, you realise you're not going to change the slide colour in year two.”

The Bellevue project is also establishing a model that can be adapted for future Mattel Wonder locations. While the brand portfolio provides a common thread, Ectovox plans to vary the attraction mix, character groupings and spatial layouts.

Martin explains: "If you go to Nebraska, you get one great experience, but if you go to Illinois, you're going to have a Mattel Wonder park with a different collection of rides and toys to play with.”

​Developing original IP and new destinations


Licensed IP is only part of Ectovox's work. The studio also develops original characters and story worlds, offering an alternative when established IP doesn't fit a project's audience, location, or commercial strategy.

Martin says: "The team are so creative in what they're developing. Chris led a project to develop a full cast of original characters, and what they have created is so exciting.

“Too many people rely on licensing what they think crowds will flock to, when they could create an emotional attachment to something truly original and never before seen, or something local that represents a culture.

“Our team has that up its sleeve, speaking back to Chris's background with Mystery Cove, where there were original characters and storylines that guests could follow.”


Grap adds that developing original IP offers a different kind of creative challenge:

"Mall of America was like an incubator in that sense because I got to work with a ton of IP in various ways, but there is passion for both things. I love working with Mattel and Hasbro, but man, do I love the 'what if' of having a space to develop an original idea.

“There are so many ideas that we cycle through, and that moment of quiet celebration the team feels when an original idea we generated clicks with a client feels so good, even before a guest gets to see it.”

Ectovox is also applying its approach to cruise ships and integrated resorts, where the team must account for different technical constraints, including vessel stability, wind loads and high guest volumes.

For cruise projects, the aquatic experience forms part of a wider day rather than an isolated attraction.

Martin says: "Cruise lines typically don't invest in licensed IP; they want to create it and own the journey. When we approach design, I approach it as someone who's going to be on that ship and experience it. We're planning for an integrated water park resort or cruise ship from eight a.m. to midnight. How do we plan that entire day?

“Our aquatics and story are a key part of their journey, and understanding passenger behaviour helps tell that guest story.”

Recent projects include Norwegian Cruise Line's Great Stirrup Cay water park expansion, Great Tides, where the aquatic development forms part of the wider destination experience.

​Designing for long-term engagement


Ectovox is looking beyond traditional water parks, with work spanning dry theme parks, family entertainment centres, themed food and beverage, resort hotels and seasonal events.

The studio is developing original IP for resort environments, including room interiors, artwork, lobby storytelling and themed bar concepts. It is also exploring how attractions can accommodate different uses throughout the year.

Planning seasonal overlays and after-dark events from the outset lets operators incorporate lighting infrastructure, sound systems, and prop anchor points into the master plan, reducing the need for major retrofits.


Grap argues that digital tools should support the physical experience rather than become the experience itself.

"There's too much reliance on trying to push tech into the park. I want people to forget their devices—make it optional to opt in, but not everything needs to go back to your cell phone.

“For years, water parks were concrete jungles with a bunch of columns and fibreglass where you didn't see much of what was happening. We're working hard to consider how guests approach certain things, giving them exciting engagement as early as possible to create a sense of life and a reason for everything.

“It's less reliance on tech, more reliance on what's happening in real life, and being intentional with it.”

For Ectovox, creative development extends beyond opening day to how destinations evolve.

Martin says:

"We want Ectovox to continue to expand beyond just the aquatic space into dry parks and facilities. Beyond that, it will be seasonal overlays and ongoing programming—what do you do with your water park after dark, or in the cold, or for Halloween and Christmas overlays? If you don't plan it on day one, it's hard to execute later.

“Our goal is to be involved with our clients for the long term, setting up that schedule, and helping them build lasting, story-driven destinations.”

title: ​Chance Rides at 65: innovation, experience and the next generation of attractions
summary:
For 65 years, Chance Rides has adapted familiar attraction formats to changing technology, markets and guest expectations. Now, as the company marks a milestone anniversary, that history provides a lens on what might shape the next 65 years.

Founded in 1961 by Harold Chance, the company began with the CP Huntington train, which would become one of its signature offerings.


Over the decades, Chance expanded into portable rides, carousels, roller coasters, people movers, observation wheels and other attractions. Its engineering and manufacturing capabilities evolved alongside that expanding portfolio.

Today, its products serve a wide range of markets and customer types, from theme parks, family entertainment centres, zoos and aquariums to travelling operators.

It is an approach Chance sees continuing into the next generation of attractions: using technology to improve the product and the experience without losing sight of the people who ultimately ride it.

​A culture of innovation


President and CEO Aaron Landrum identifies the development of the CP Huntington as a defining moment in Chance's history. The next major shift came with portability.

“That was a fundamental shift when, at that time, the industry was taking days or weeks to set up a ride. Now it got down to a day or two. Chance really was at the forefront of that evolution of portability for showmen.”


Portability changed the commercial possibilities for travelling operators, while also establishing a pattern that would recur throughout Chance's history: applying its engineering and manufacturing capabilities to new markets.

“In the 80s, we got into the carousel business, a whole new product line. In the 90s, we started developing people movers, trams. Then we got into observation wheels.”

The company's development continued into the 2000s, including the acquisition of D.H. Morgan, while more recent years have brought international partnerships, including with EVX Mobility in Sweden.

Along the way, individual products marked important steps in that evolution, from the trailer-mounted Trabant to the Superman coaster built for Six Flags Mexico.

“That culture of constant innovation was a defining feature over 65 years.”

The result is a portfolio that spans very different attraction formats, but shares a common foundation in engineering, manufacturing and long-term product development.

​Engineering the ride before it is built


The technology behind that development has changed significantly.

Jeremy McClanahan, operations manager at Chance Rides, says the move from traditional two-dimensional drawings to three-dimensional engineering has transformed the design process.

“That transition has allowed us to simulate, validate, and refine our designs long before the first parts are produced.”

Manufacturing has evolved alongside engineering, with CNC equipment, improved fabrication processes, and greater automation improving consistency and quality.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Chance Rides, LLC (@chanceridesllc)

However, for Travis Lane, project management director, these technologies matter for more than producing a more precise piece of machinery. They change how much of the design work can happen before manufacturing begins.

“A lot of it now is upfront. It's anticipatory,” he says. “When you have those powerful modelling tools and software that allow you to make a rapid change, as opposed to, hey, we are committed to this print, or even we're committed to this delivery date, and we have to release a ride right now.”

title: Tokyo Disneyland sets opening date for new 'Wreck-It Ralph' ride
summary:
Tokyo Disneyland has set an opening date for its new Wreck-It Ralph ride, Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue.

The world’s first Wreck-It Ralph-themed attraction will officially open on 15 April, 2027 at Tokyo Disneyland, coinciding with the theme park's 44th anniversary.

A redesign of the park's former Buzz Lightyear interactive dark ride, Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue invites guests on an adventure alongside Ralph and Vanellope to defeat King Candy.

Tokyo Disneyland’s new Pixel Prism shop will feature pixel-patterned flooring, fibre optic-inspired designs and attraction merchandiseDisney

In the new attraction, King Candy is plotting to take over the world of video games and has transformed the candies of Sugar Rush into Sugar Bugs programmed to consume the whole kingdom.

On the new ride, guests will enter the Sugar Rush game world from the Wreck-It Ralph films, teaming up with Ralph and Vanellope to restore the Sugar Bugs to their original kawaii forms before they destroy everything.

The ride will let guests scan the bugs using devices onboard ride vehicles, transforming them back to their original forms. Points will be awarded based on the types and number of Sugar Bugs restored.

Riders will be able to view their results on the ride vehicle screens and, for a limited time, in the Tokyo Disney Resort app, where ride photos will also be available to purchase.

Tokyo Disneyland’s Tomorrowland expansion includes Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue, Space Mountain Earthrise and new shopping and dining optionsDisney

Outside the ride, Pixel Prism, a new shop selling Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue merchandise, will also open on 15 April 2027.

Popping Station, a new popcorn stand overlooking Tomorrowland Plaza, will open on 17 March, serving Sugar-Lime Popcorn inspired by the attraction.

Ahead of the attraction’s opening, a Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue-inspired smartphone mini-game will launch on 12 January, followed by themed decorations and photo opportunities in Tomorrowland in February and Cinderella Castle projections in March.

Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue will join the new Space Mountain Earthrise indoor roller coaster, also opening in 2027, as part of a 100 billion yen ($630 million) transformation of Tokyo Disneyland’s Tomorrowland.

title: Disney invests $1m in Jane Goodall’s youth conservation programme
summary:
The Disney Conservation Fund has announced a $1 million investment in Roots & Shoots, the Jane Goodall Institute's youth programme.

The investment will support Roots & Shoots, which was created to inspire young people to identify challenges in their communities and take action for people, animals and the environment.

Founded in 1991 by the late Jane Goodall, Roots & Shoots is now active in 75 countries, including all 50 US states and Puerto Rico.

Goodall, a British primatologist and conservationist, was a trailblazer known for her pioneering studies of chimpanzees.

An advocate for conservation and community-led change, Goodall spent more than four decades advancing the Jane Goodall Institute's programmes in Africa and around the world.

The Disney Conservation Fund is committed to inspiring action and connecting children with natureDisney

Disney's investment builds on its conservation fund's longstanding commitment to inspiring action and connecting children with nature.

The announcement comes as 10 youth conservation leaders from across the US gathered at Walt Disney World Resort for a multi-day conservation summit celebrating youth action and environmental stewardship.

Selected earlier this year through the 'Hop into the Animal Kingdom Challenge', created in collaboration with Roots & Shoots USA, these youth advocates are leading projects focused on wildlife conservation, habitat restoration, environmental education, pollution reduction and community engagement.

"The future of conservation depends on supporting and inspiring the next generation of leaders," said Claire Martin, senior manager of biodiversity conservation programmes at the Walt Disney Company.

Roots & Shoots investment

"By connecting young people with nature and giving them opportunities to explore careers in animal care, conservation and science, we can help inspire lifelong champions for wildlife and the planet," she added.

"We’re proud to collaborate with Jane Goodall’s Roots & Shoots to celebrate these remarkable young leaders and invest in the future of conservation."

title: How Gateway Ticketing Systems is putting live ticket inventory into agentic commerce
summary:
Ticketing has changed significantly over the past three decades. Physical ticket booths and paper passes have given way to online booking, mobile tickets and increasingly sophisticated distribution networks.

Now, another shift is underway.

As AI becomes part of how consumers search for and plan experiences, attractions may increasingly find themselves selling through a different kind of intermediary: an AI agent acting on a guest's behalf.

These agents could research itineraries, compare products and prices and eventually complete transactions, raising new questions about how attractions structure their data and make inventory available.

For operators, the implications could extend beyond booking. As AI agents take on more of the searching and comparing, the quality and accessibility of an attraction's data could become as important as its website or checkout flow.

To explore what agentic commerce could mean for the visitor attractions industry, blooloop spoke to Kori Richards, group product manager, and Becky Lathrop, senior manager for software development, at Gateway Ticketing Systems, Inc.


With more than 450 venues across six continents using its admission control and ticketing technology, Gateway Ticketing Systems has spent decades working at the intersection of attractions, ticketing and distribution.

The company’s experience with APIs, third-party distributors and real-time inventory gives Richards and Lathrop a practical perspective on what an AI-driven distribution model requires.

Although agentic commerce is still in its early stages, they argue that attractions should start preparing now by considering how their systems, data and distribution infrastructure can adapt.

​AI as a distribution channel


For many attractions, AI in ticketing still means a customer-support chatbot answering questions on a website. Richards and Lathrop see a much broader opportunity.

"There are two things that people are calling agentic commerce," says Richards. "One is a conversational assistant that lives on your own website. It answers questions, sells tickets, and acts as your personal concierge, and that's more of a conversion tool.

“The other is making your live inventory available and discoverable across different AI platforms, such as Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT, so that someone can find your tickets or your attraction and buy them in a conversation that you don't own on your website.”


The shift moves the focus from how an attraction's website looks to a human visitor to how its ticketing system can be understood by an AI agent.

In an agentic commerce model, an AI agent operates on a guest's behalf. A guest might ask their AI assistant to find a wildlife attraction for a family of four, within a set budget and timeframe, then book it and add it to their itinerary.

The agent can then identify suitable attractions, check availability and pricing, and complete the transaction without the guest visiting the attraction's website.

Lathrop says this shift is driven by rapid changes in guest behaviour:

"There are new ways that our guests are reaching for information. There's a new generation that is going to ChatGPT rather than Google. There's a shift happening, and we want to make sure that our customers are there to meet them.”

​Gateway's AI Commerce


Gateway Ticketing Systems has built this second model into a product called AI Commerce.

The product connects an attraction's live Galaxy pricing and availability to AI platforms including Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing a guest to find an attraction, check a date and buy tickets inside a conversation the attraction does not host.


Operators choose which products are exposed and where, plus additional sales opportunities. The AI layer never handles card data, and every price and availability check runs against Galaxy in real time.

AI Commerce is in production with early customers, with general availability to follow.

From SEO to AEO​


For decades, digital marketing in the attractions industry has focused heavily on Search Engine Optimisation (SEO). As visitors increasingly use AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to find information, operators may also need to consider how their content appears in AI-generated answers.

Rather than receiving a list of search results, visitors may receive a synthesised answer. This has prompted growing interest in Answer Engine Optimisation (AEO) and what it could mean for attractions' digital strategies.


This increases the importance of making key information, including ticket prices, operating hours and availability, accessible to AI systems. If machines can't easily interpret important information, an attraction may be harder for an AI agent to discover or transact with.

To bridge the communication gap between ticketing systems and large language models, the tech industry has begun adopting open standards.

"Rather than just surfacing APIs available, [we are] making it easier for the capabilities, and then also putting real-world safeguards to it as well," says Lathrop. "In the past month, there's been a standard released on MCPs, and this is something that we've adopted.”

The MCP provides a standardised way for AI applications to connect with external tools and data. For ticketing systems, this could reduce the need for bespoke integrations between individual platforms and make it easier for AI agents to access capabilities, inventory and rates.

​The new personalisation


Personalisation has long been part of attraction e-commerce, with platforms using past purchases and customer data to predict what a guest might want next.

Agentic commerce changes that model: instead of a platform guessing what a guest might want, the guest can tell their AI assistant what they need.

"The traditional personalisation is making educated guesses on what you might want next, and putting an offer in front of you, and hoping that it's attractive enough for you to take it," Richards says. "With an assistant, the guest is telling you what they need. That changes what the platform needs to be good at.”


The ticketing platform must then verify those requirements against real-time operational data, she adds:

"Is that time slot that they are looking for really truly available, or is this just something that you wanted to push the guest towards? Is the price for that group on that date, with their membership applied, valid?”

​​The benefits of agentic commerce for operators


The potential applications extend beyond the guest-facing journey.

Gateway Ticketing Systems is also exploring how AI can make complex ticketing data easier for operators to access, including through its Galaxy software.

"We've also changed this approach for us by allowing a back-office MCP to surface the analytical data configuration information that's available in the cloud right to our customers so that they can manage right from their phone," Lathrop says.

"This will hopefully result in frictionless transactions with our guests.”


AI agents could also support back-office tasks such as inventory management, pricing analysis, waitlist fulfilment, refunds, exchanges and customer support. By offloading these routine tasks to automated systems, attractions can free their staff to focus on higher-value, face-to-face guest interactions.

However, Richards raises a critical point about the limits of AI prediction: it is only as good as the underlying data. Many attractions are still building out the basic operational data required to feed an AI model.

"The interesting blocker about that isn't necessarily the AI piece," Richards says.

"It's a much simpler question that attractions need to answer: how many people are on your site right now, how many are across in parking and across the gate? Prediction is the last piece, not the first. You have to have some type of data to back that up, and attractions are still getting onto that as well.”

Without reliable operational data, however, AI predictions will be limited.

​Connecting systems with Gateway Ticketing Systems


Gateway's experience connecting attractions with external distributors provides a useful precedent for its AI approach. Its Galaxy Connect platform was designed to solve the same basic many-to-many problem: allowing an attraction to make its inventory available across multiple channels without maintaining a separate integration for each one.

"In the pre-AI world, it was all API calls, and there were specific interactions that you could do," says Lathrop.

"Where you have the flexibility of having an agent discussing with MCPs the capabilities and surfacing the data underneath without the strict calls back and forth, it's really providing that flexibility for those interactions to more naturally come together as a person would."


Galaxy Connect has around 135 certified distributors, including Expedia, Viator and GetYourGuide. Rather than maintaining individual integrations with each partner, an attraction can connect once to access the wider network.

"And so, this is a new type of intermediary that we're solving for again on the AI front," Richards adds.

The comparison offers one way to think about the next stage of distribution. Just as attractions have needed to connect inventory to multiple online travel agencies, they may increasingly need to make that inventory accessible to AI agents.

The technology may be different, but the underlying challenge is familiar: making products, availability and pricing accessible across an increasingly fragmented distribution landscape.

​Avoiding transactional friction


AI discussions often focus on upselling, from higher-value tickets to dining packages and other add-ons. Richards argues that the bigger opportunity may be recovering sales lost through transactional friction.

"What's interesting about this is that I gently push back that revenue comes from upselling directly. The bigger number here is about the sale that you're losing.”

Attraction e-commerce journeys can involve significant friction. When guests drop out of the purchasing process, it is rarely because the system failed to suggest an upsell. Instead, they may abandon their carts because of transactional friction.


Richards lists the primary drivers of this lost revenue:

"Perhaps not trusting your site with the card that you're using or the payment method, being forced to create an account on the website could deter guests or visitors as well. A checkout that's taking too long, things of that nature. Almost none of it is a failure to suggest something extra at that point.”

Agentic commerce could reduce some of these barriers by allowing an AI assistant to handle parts of the purchasing process on the guest's behalf.

​Security, access, and control


Giving AI access to any part of the transaction process also raises questions about security, accuracy and control. What happens if an AI invents a discount, sells a ticket for a closed day or accesses information it should not see?

Richards and Lathrop argue that operators should control what AI systems can access and how they can use it.

Gateway Ticketing Systems has built several guardrails into its approach to AI commerce, starting with the principle that operators choose exactly which products and information are made available.

"We've made a few decisions early on," Lathrop says. "By default, every storefront has to be turned on individually. There's no enable everything button. The operator picks what's exposed and just deliberately determines what can be surfaced to AI."

That means a venue could choose to test an AI-powered channel with a limited number of ticket types or timeslots before making more of its inventory available.

Payment security is another consideration. Gateway Ticketing Systems’ architecture keeps the AI layer separate from payment-card data, with transactions completed through the attraction's existing certified checkout, Lathrop says.

"It never touches card data," says Lathrop.

"The AI layer is hands-off to the operator's existing certified checkout. This keeps PCI in scope, and the path has already been certified. And it means that guests pay somewhere where they recognise and they understand it."


The same separation applies to personal data.

"We don't collect that data in the chat. They may know that person from their own interactions with their own ChatGPT in the memory, but that never comes into our commerce interaction, and it doesn't go between."

Pricing and availability present another challenge, particularly for attractions managing capacity-controlled inventory.

Gateway Ticketing Systems’ approach is to pull rates and availability from the core Galaxy ticketing system rather than allowing the AI to make assumptions based on cached or incomplete information.

"Prices and availability come from the existing pricing and inventory, and it never places inventory holds until they're ready to check out," Lathrop says.

"If the information is unavailable, the system returns an error rather than guessing. An assistant must never tell guests something is sold out when a pricing service just failed.

"Our internal target for overselling or overcharging through this surface is zero, and that's a design constraint, not an aspiration."

There is also a legal question that technology alone cannot solve: who is accountable when an AI gives a guest the wrong information?

Lathrop points to the Air Canada chatbot case, in which the airline was held responsible for incorrect information its chatbot provided.

"For operators, the question is asking: what data is leaving my environment, and who's getting it, and can I switch it off immediately? And is the guest clearly told they're talking to AI? And who's responsible when something's going wrong?"

As attractions experiment with AI-powered commerce, this question of control is likely to become increasingly important. For Gateway Ticketing Systems, the key point is that an AI agent does not take responsibility away from the attraction using it.

​Good bots, bad bots


One challenge of agentic commerce is distinguishing between "good" bots and "bad" bots.

Ticketing platforms have spent years defending against bots that scrape sites, lock up inventory or buy tickets for resale. Agentic commerce presents the opposite challenge: opening systems to legitimate AI agents acting on behalf of guests.

"Treating the chat window as the new strategy is a common misconception," Richards says.

"A chatbot is an interface. Agentic commerce is a question about distribution and data. You can buy a really good chat interface and still be completely invisible to that AI agent because your prices, your availability aren't machine-readable or discoverable."


The regulatory framework around distinguishing legitimate consumer AI agents from prohibited ticket bots is also still developing.

"There's no regulatory answer to that yet," Richards says. "No FTC guidance, no case law, so nothing that's really distinguishing a guest's own shopping assistant from a prohibited ticket bot."

That means operators will need clear policies around automated access, supported by tools such as authentication, monitoring and rate limiting.

"Decide your bot policy on purpose too," Lathrop says. "What does get automated? ... Tag the channel so that you can measure it."

The challenge, then, is not simply how to stop bots. As agentic commerce develops, attractions will need to decide which bots they are prepared to let in.

​Practical advice


With technology and standards evolving quickly, attractions may find it difficult to know where to start.

Richards and Lathrop suggest focusing on four fundamentals.

Firstly, start with the basics. A fast, mobile-friendly website and well-structured data are essential. "If your site takes 25 seconds to load on a phone, you're not ready for AI agents," Richards says. "Speed and structured data for sure are the foundation, and they help your human guests as well."

Create a single source of truth. If an attraction's website, OTA feeds and other sales channels show different prices or availability, adding an AI channel will only compound the problem.

"Just the source of truth for price and availability," Richards says. "If your OTA feed and your website disagree on what's available on a Saturday or have different pricing, adding a fourth channel to that is not going to make anything easier."

Additionally, measure and manage automated sales. Operators should decide which AI interactions to allow and tag agent-generated transactions so they can measure performance.


Finally, they advise operators to stay flexible. With standards still evolving, attractions should avoid locking themselves into a single AI platform or proprietary format.

"Work with something open and adaptable," Richards advises. "Nobody knows whether the winning standard ... is right now OpenAI or ChatGPT or Google or MCP. Anybody that tells you that they know the answer is selling you something because it is very much the Wild West."

The priority, therefore, is less about predicting which platform will win and more about ensuring underlying systems can adapt.

The direction of travel may still be uncertain, but the underlying requirements are becoming clearer. Attractions will need accurate data, connected systems and clear policies around automated access if they are to participate in an increasingly AI-driven distribution landscape.

Gateway Ticketing Systems has spent decades connecting attractions with ticketing and distribution systems, so agentic commerce represents the next stage of a challenge it already knows well: making attraction inventory accessible across an increasingly complex digital ecosystem.

With AI Commerce, the company is applying that experience to a new generation of distribution, putting live ticketing data within reach of the AI agents that may increasingly shape how guests discover and buy attractions.

title: How to maintain coasters and attractions: strategy, culture & OEM partnerships
summary:
Attraction maintenance isn't a glamorous job. Stripping down a complex ride system outdoors in the middle of a British winter is not something that sells itself on a recruitment poster.

Yet across theme parks worldwide, maintaining roller coasters and complex rides has quietly become one of the industry's most pressing challenges.


Our experts

Jamie Gaffney

Partnerships are crucial to the success of any multi-stakeholder project.— Lee Hollinshead, D-Tex Visual Ltd

title: Comcast Q3: Theme Parks revenue falls 4% driven by weaker Orlando and Japan
summary:
Universal parent company Comcast reported its third-quarter 2026 earnings, confirming that theme parks revenue and adjusted EBITDA fell 4.4 per cent and 17.1 per cent year on year, respectively, as softer demand in Orlando and Japan weighed on results.

Speaking on the company's earnings call, president and co-chief executive officer Mike Cavanagh attributed Orlando's weakness to "macroeconomic and geopolitical headwinds".

Cavanagh said two other factors had "contributed to this recent softness" compared with 2025.

He said competitors were quicker to adapt their marketing strategies to softer demand, while Universal faced difficult comparisons after the June 2025 opening of Epic Universe, which boosted attendance.

Epic Universe boosted Universal attendance after opening in June 2025, creating tougher comparisons for Comcast in 2026 Universal

Universal is working to address capacity challenges and improve ride throughput at Epic Universe, which Cavanagh described as "the most technologically advanced theme park ever built".

He said improvements included "getting the tech settled down" and training staff to load and unload rides at the right speed.

In Japan, Comcast chief financial officer Jason Armstrong said: "China-related travel restrictions continue to weigh on attendance".

To respond to softer demand, Universal plans to introduce promotional offers and product packages, including three-park passes in Orlando, alongside increased marketing investment.

The company has also strengthened its leadership team. Luc Bondar, formerly of United Airlines, has joined as chief brand and commercial officer, while former NBCUniversal CFO Randy Culbertson is joining Universal Destinations & Experiences as chief business officer.

Comcast expects Universal Studios Hollywood to benefit from the new Fast & Furious coaster following its recent opening Universal

Looking ahead, Armstrong said: "We expect to begin lapping the initial pressure in Japan in the fourth quarter, while Hollywood should benefit from the recent opening of the new Fast & Furious coaster.

"However, softer demand and difficult comparisons in Orlando are expected to remain headwinds to overall theme park results in the fourth quarter."

Cavanagh said Orlando attendance, per-capita guest spending and overall financial performance remained materially above levels seen two years ago, while guest satisfaction continued to rise.

The company expects theme parks performance to return to growth in the second half of 2027.
